law-of-contract-i-u1-t1.subtitle: Sections 2(e), 2(h) and 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A contract is an agreement that the law will enforce (Section 2(h)). An agreement is born when one person makes a proposal and the other accepts it (Sections 2(a), 2(b), 2(e)). Not every agreement is a contract. Section 10 says an agreement becomes a contract only when it is made with free consent , by competent parties , for a lawful consideration , with a lawful object , and is not expressly declared void . Courts add one more: the parties must intend to create legal relations ( Balfour v. Balfour ). So remember the line: all contracts are agreements, but all agreements are not contracts. In exams, marks come from listing every essential, giving the section for each, and adding one case or example for each. In real life, this checklist tells you whether a promise can be taken to court.
legalProvision: Section 2. In this Act the following words and expressions are used in the following senses, unless a contrary intention appears from the context:— (a) When one person signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other to such act or abstinence, he is said to make a proposal; (b) When the person to whom the proposal is made signifies his assent thereto, the proposal is said to be accepted. A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise; (c) The person making the proposal is called the "promisor", and the person accepting the proposal is called the "promisee"; (d) When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise; (e) Every promise and every set of promises, forming the consideration for each other, is an agreement; (f) Promises which form the consideration or part of the consideration for each other are called reciprocal promises; (g) An agreement not enforceable by law is said to be void; (h) An agreement enforceable by law is a contract; (i) An agreement which is enforceable by law at the option of one or more of the parties thereto, but not at the option of the other or others, is a voidable contract; (j) A contract which ceases to be enforceable by law becomes void when it ceases to be enforceable.

Section 10. What agreements are contracts. All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void. Nothing herein contained shall affect any law in force in India and not hereby expressly repealed by which any contract is required to be made in writing or in the presence of witnesses, or any law relating to the registration of documents.

Section 11. Who are competent to contract. Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.
Section 13. "Consent" defined. Two or more persons are said to consent when they agree upon the same thing in the same sense.

Section 14. "Free consent" defined. Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by— (1) coercion, as defined in section 15, or (2) undue influence, as defined in section 16, or (3) fraud, as defined in section 17, or (4) misrepresentation, as defined in section 18, or (5) mistake, subject to the provisions of sections 20, 21 and 22.
In simple words

Section 2(a)–(b): a proposal (offer) is made; when it is accepted , it becomes a promise . Section 2(c): the one who proposes is the promisor ; the one who accepts is the promisee . Section 2(e): a promise, or set of promises, given for each other is an agreement . Section 2(h): an agreement the law will enforce is a contract . Section 2(g), (i), (j): some agreements are void from the start; some contracts are voidable at one party's option; a valid contract can later become void . Section 10: lists what turns an agreement into a contract. Sections 11, 13, 14: explain "competent", "consent" and "free consent".
en.meaning:
The two-step formula The Act builds the definition in two steps. Agreement = offer + acceptance . A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise (Section 2(b)). Every promise forming the consideration for each other is an agreement (Section 2(e)). Contract = agreement + enforceability by law. An agreement enforceable by law is a contract (Section 2(h)). Promises forming consideration for each other are an agreement (Section 2(e)). If the law enforces the agreement it is a contract (Section 2(h)); if not, it is a void agreement (Section 2(g)). Definitions by writers Writers on contract law give similar definitions. Two are often quoted in exams: Pollock: "Every agreement and promise enforceable at law is a contract." Anson: a contract is a legally binding agreement between two or more persons by which rights are acquired by one or more to acts or forbearances on the part of the other or others. Both say the same thing as Section 2(h): agreement + legal enforceability . "All contracts are agreements, but all agreements are not contracts" A contract is always an agreement. But an agreement is a contract only if it meets the Section 10 conditions. A social or domestic promise (to go to a film, to give pocket money) is an agreement but usually not a contract, because the parties did not mean it to go to court. Why the law has these essentials The law enforces a promise only when it is fair and sensible to do so. Each essential protects someone: Free consent protects a person who was forced or cheated. Capacity protects minors and persons of unsound mind. Consideration separates a bargain from a bare promise. Lawful object protects society from illegal deals. Intention to create legal relations keeps family and social promises out of court. Running example Anil offers to sell his used laptop to Bhavana for ₹30,000 . Bhavana accepts. She pays an advance of ₹5,000 today and promises to pay the balance ₹25,000 (₹30,000 − ₹5,000) on delivery next Monday. We will test this deal against every essential below. At the end, we will see what happens if one essential is missing.
keyPoints: Contract = agreement + enforceability by law (Section 2(h)). Agreement = offer + acceptance (Sections 2(a), 2(b), 2(e)). Section 10: free consent, competent parties, lawful consideration, lawful object, not expressly declared void. Intention to create legal relations is added by courts ( Balfour v. Balfour ). Competence: majority, sound mind, not disqualified (Section 11); a minor's agreement is void ( Mohori Bibee ). Consent without freedom makes a contract voidable ; mutual mistake of fact makes an agreement void . Uncertain (Section 29) and impossible (Section 56) agreements are void. Writing is needed only where a law requires it (Section 10, second paragraph).

caseLaws.name: Balfour v
caseLaws.facts: Balfour (1919) Facts. A husband who held a government post in Ceylon promised his wife £30 a month when she had to stay in England on medical advice. They later separated, and she sued for the allowance. Principle. Agreements between husband and wife made in the ordinary domestic relationship are generally not contracts, because the parties do not intend them to be attended by legal consequences. [1919] 2 KB 571 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It is the leading case on intention to create legal relations in domestic agreements. Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893) Facts. The company advertised a £100 reward to anyone who caught influenza after using its smoke ball three times daily for two weeks, and deposited £1,000 with the Alliance Bank to show its sincerity. Mrs Carlill used the ball as directed and caught influenza. Principle. An offer may be made to the world at large and accepted by anyone who performs its conditions; the deposit showed an intention to be bound. [1893] 1 QB 256 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It shows offer, acceptance by performance and intention to create legal relations together. Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903) Facts. Dharmodas Ghose, while a minor, mortgaged his houses to a money-lender, Brahmo Dutt, to secure Rs. 20,000. The lender's agent had notice that he was a minor. Principle. A minor is not competent to contract under Section 11, so a minor's agreement is void, not voidable. (1903) LR 30 IA 114 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It settles the capacity essential and the void–voidable distinction for minors. Rose and Frank Co. v. J.R. Crompton and Bros. Ltd. (1925) Facts. English makers of carbon paper and their American distributor, Rose and Frank, signed an arrangement in 1913 which said it was not a formal or legal agreement and was only an honourable pledge. Later the makers refused some orders. Principle. In business agreements intention is presumed, but clear words can exclude it; the 1913 arrangement itself was not enforceable, though orders actually given and accepted under it were. [1925] AC 445 (House of Lords). Why it matters. It shows that the commercial presumption can be rebutted by express words.

law-of-contract-i-u1-t2.subtitle: Sections 2(a), 2(c), 4 and 29 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Every contract starts with an offer . The Act calls it a proposal . Under Section 2(a), a person makes a proposal when he signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other . A valid offer must be definite , must be made with the intention of being bound on acceptance , and must be communicated to the person who is to accept it. It must be different from an invitation to offer , such as a price list, a shop display, an advertisement for an auction, or a call for tenders. In exams, marks come from the definition, the list of essentials with a case for each, and the offer versus invitation-to-offer distinction ( Harvey v. Facey , MacPherson v. Appanna ). In real life, this decides whether you can say "I accept" and hold the other person to a bargain.
legalProvision: Section 2(a). When one person signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other to such act or abstinence, he is said to make a proposal;
Section 2(b). When the person to whom the proposal is made signifies his assent thereto, the proposal is said to be accepted. A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise;
Section 2(c). The person making the proposal is called the "promisor", and the person accepting the proposal is called the "promisee";

Section 3. Communication, acceptance and revocation of proposals. The communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, and the revocation of proposals and acceptances, respectively, are deemed to be made by any act or omission of the party proposing, accepting or revoking by which he intends to communicate such proposal, acceptance or revocation, or which has the effect of communicating it.

Section 4 (first paragraph). The communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made. Illustration (a): A proposes, by letter, to sell a house to B at a certain price. The communication of the proposal is complete when B receives the letter.

Section 8. Acceptance by performing conditions, or receiving consideration. Performance of the conditions of a proposal, or the acceptance of any consideration for a reciprocal promise which may be offered with a proposal, is an acceptance of the proposal.

Section 9. Promises, express and implied. In so far as the proposal or acceptance of any promise is made in words, the promise is said to be express. In so far as such proposal or acceptance is made otherwise than in words, the promise is said to be implied.
Section 29. Agreements void for uncertainty. Agreements, the meaning of which is not certain, or capable of being made certain, are void.
In simple words

Section 2(a): an offer is a willingness to do or not do something, shown to another person, in order to get his "yes" . Section 2(b), (c): when that "yes" comes, the offer becomes a promise . The offeror is the promisor ; the acceptor is the promisee . Section 3: an offer can be made by words or conduct (any act or omission meant to communicate it). Section 4: an offer is communicated only when it comes to the knowledge of the offeree. Section 8: some offers are accepted by doing what they ask (useful for offers to the public). Section 9: an offer in words is express ; one made by conduct is implied . Section 29: an offer so vague that no certain agreement can come out of it produces a void agreement.
en.meaning:
Offer and proposal mean the same thing

The Act uses the word proposal . English law and most textbooks use offer . They mean the same thing. The person who makes it is the offeror (proposer, promisor). The person to whom it is made is the offeree (promisee once he accepts).

Section 2(a) broken into parts

Words of Section 2(a) What it means Example "When one person signifies to another" The offer must be shown (communicated) to another person Meena writes to Ravi "his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything" It can be an offer to do or not to do something To sell a sewing machine; or not to open a rival shop "with a view to obtaining the assent of that other" It is made to get the other's acceptance , with an intention to be bound if he accepts "Will you buy it for ₹8,000?"

Why the law needs a clear offer

A contract is formed the moment an offer is accepted. So the law must be able to point to one definite offer whose acceptance closes the deal. If every price list, advertisement or enquiry were an offer, a shopkeeper could be bound to sell to a thousand people the same item. That is why the law separates a true offer from a mere invitation to offer .

Running example

Meena writes a letter to Ravi : "I will sell you my sewing machine, model XL-200, for ₹8,000 . Delivery at my house on Sunday. Please reply by Friday."

We will test this letter against every essential below.
keyPoints: Offer = proposal (Section 2(a)): willingness to do or abstain, shown to another, to obtain his assent . It must be made with an intention to be bound on acceptance. It must be definite (Section 29). It must be communicated ; communication is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the offeree (Section 4). An invitation to offer (display, price list, auction notice, tender notice, quotation) is not an offer. A general offer can be accepted by anyone who knows of it and performs its conditions (Section 8; Carlill ). Offers may be express or implied (Section 9). Silence cannot be made acceptance ( Felthouse v. Bindley ).

caseLaws.name: Harvey v
caseLaws.facts: Facey (1893) Facts. Harvey telegraphed asking whether Facey would sell Bumper Hall Pen and his lowest cash price. Facey replied "Lowest price for Bumper Hall Pen £900." Harvey telegraphed that he agreed to buy at £900; Facey did not reply. Principle. A statement of the lowest price in reply to an enquiry is not an offer to sell. Harvey's last telegram was only an offer, never accepted. [1893] AC 552 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It is the leading case separating an offer from a mere quotation of price. MacPherson v. M.N. Appanna (1951) Facts. The owner of a bungalow in Mercara, told of an offer of Rs. 6,000, cabled "Won't accept less than rupees ten thousand." Appanna wrote to confirm his offer of ten thousand; the owner sold to another for Rs. 11,000. Principle. A statement of the lowest price at which one would sell is not an offer; there was no concluded contract. AIR 1951 SC 184 : 1951 SCR 161. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court's adoption of Harvey v. Facey in India. Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893) Facts. The company advertised a £100 reward to anyone who caught influenza after using its smoke ball three times daily for two weeks, and deposited £1,000 with a bank. Mrs Carlill used it as directed and caught influenza. Principle. An offer can be made to the world at large; it is accepted by anyone who performs the conditions, and notice of acceptance can be dispensed with. [1893] 1 QB 256 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It is the leading case on general offers . Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt (1913) Facts. A servant was sent to search for his master's missing nephew. While he was away, the master announced a reward. The servant found the boy and later claimed the reward. Principle. A person who does the act without knowing of the offer cannot claim to have accepted it. Allahabad High Court, 1913. Why it matters. It shows that an offer must be communicated (known) before it can be accepted. Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v. Boots Cash Chemists (Southern) Ltd. (1953) Facts. Boots let customers pick certain medicines from open shelves and pay at a cash desk, where a pharmacist supervised. The Society said the sale took place at the shelf, without supervision. Principle. Display of goods is an invitation to offer. The customer offers to buy at the cash desk, and the seller accepts there. [1953] 1 QB 401 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It is the leading case on display of goods . Felthouse v. Bindley (1862) Facts. An uncle offered to buy his nephew's horse for £30 15s, writing that if he heard no more he would consider the horse his. The nephew did not reply; the horse was sold at auction by mistake. Principle. An offeror cannot make the offeree's silence an acceptance. 142 ER 1037 : (1862) 11 CB (NS) 869. Why it matters. It limits what conditions an offeror can put in an offer.

selfTest.q: 1. What does the Act call an offer?
selfTest.a: A proposal (Section 2(a)).

selfTest.q: 2. Is a reply stating "lowest price ₹9 lakh" an offer?
selfTest.a: No. It is a statement of price ( Harvey v. Facey ; MacPherson v. Appanna ).

selfTest.q: 3. When is the communication of an offer complete?
selfTest.a: When it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made (Section 4).

selfTest.q: 4. Can a person who returns a lost article without knowing of the reward claim it?
selfTest.a: No. He did not know of the offer ( Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt ).

selfTest.q: 5. Are goods on a supermarket shelf an offer?
selfTest.a: No. They are an invitation to offer; the customer offers at the counter ( Boots ).

selfTest.q: 6. Can an offeror say "your silence will mean acceptance"?
selfTest.a: He can say it, but it does not bind the offeree ( Felthouse v. Bindley ).

law-of-contract-i-u1-t4.subtitle: Sections 3, 4 and 9 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872; section 13 of the Information Technology Act, 2000

en.inOneMinute: An offer and an acceptance work only when they are communicated . Section 3 says communication may be by any act or omission meant to communicate, or which has that effect. Section 4 fixes the moment each communication is complete: a proposal is communicated when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made; an acceptance is complete against the proposer when it is put in a course of transmission to him (for example, posted), and against the acceptor when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer. So in a contract by post, the proposer is bound as soon as the letter of acceptance is posted. For instantaneous means (face to face, telephone, telex), the courts apply the ordinary rule: the contract is made when and where the acceptance is received ( Entores ; Bhagwandas Goverdhandas Kedia ). Contracts by email are valid ( Trimex ; IT Act, Section 10A), and the IT Act fixes when and where an electronic message is sent and received (Section 13). In exams, marks come from Section 4 quoted with its illustrations, the two-stage rule for acceptance, the postal and telephone cases, and the place of contract. In real life, it decides when you are bound and which court can hear the case.
legalProvision: Section 3. Communication, acceptance and revocation of proposals. The communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, and the revocation of proposals and acceptances, respectively, are deemed to be made by any act or omission of the party proposing, accepting or revoking by which he intends to communicate such proposal, acceptance or revocation, or which has the effect of communicating it.

Section 4. Communication when complete. The communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made. The communication of an acceptance is complete,— as against the proposer, when it is put in a course of transmission to him, so as to be out of the power of the acceptor; as against the acceptor, when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer. The communication of a revocation is complete,— as against the person who makes it, when it is put into a course of transmission to the person to whom it is made, so as to be out of the power of the person who makes it; as against the person to whom it is made, when it comes to his knowledge. Illustrations (a) A proposes, by letter, to sell a house to B at a certain price. The communication of the proposal is complete when B receives the letter. (b) B accepts A's proposal by a letter sent by post. The communication of the acceptance is complete, as against A when the letter is posted; as against B, when the letter is received by A. (c) A revokes his proposal by telegram. The revocation is complete as against A when the telegram is despatched. It is complete as against B when B receives it. B revokes his acceptance by telegram. B's revocation is complete as against B when the telegram is despatched, and as against A when it reaches him.

Section 5 (first two paragraphs). A proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer, but not afterwards. An acceptance may be revoked at any time before the communication of the acceptance is complete as against the acceptor, but not afterwards.
Information Technology Act, 2000

Section 10A. Validity of contracts formed through electronic means. Where in a contract formation, the communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, the revocation of proposals and acceptances, as the case may be, are expressed in electronic form or by means of an electronic records, such contract shall not be deemed to be unenforceable solely on the ground that such electronic form or means was used for that purpose.

Section 13. Time and place of despatch and receipt of electronic record. (1) Save as otherwise agreed to between the originator and the addressee, the despatch of an electronic record occurs when it enters a computer resource outside the control of the originator. (2) Save as otherwise agreed between the originator and the addressee, the time of receipt of an electronic record shall be determined as follows, namely:– (a) if the addressee has designated a computer resource for the purpose of receiving electronic records,– (i) receipt occurs at the time when the electronic record enters the designated computer resource; or (ii) if the electronic record is sent to a computer resource of the addressee that is not the designated computer resource, receipt occurs at the time when the electronic record is retrieved by the addressee; (b) if the addressee has not designated a computer resource along with specified timings, if any, receipt occurs when the electronic record enters the computer resource of the addressee. (3) Save as otherwise agreed to between the originator and the addressee, an electronic record is deemed to be despatched at the place where the originator has his place of business, and is deemed to be received at the place where the addressee has his place of business. (4) The provisions of sub-section (2) shall apply notwithstanding that the place where the computer resource is located may be different from the place where the electronic record is deemed to have been received under sub-section (3). (5) For the purposes of this section,– (a) if the originator or the addressee has more than one place of business, the principal place of business, shall be the place of business; (b) if the originator or the addressee does not have a place of business, his usual place of residence shall be deemed to be the place of business; (c) "usual place of residence", in relation to a body corporate, means the place where it is registered.
Sections 11 (attribution) and 12 (acknowledgment of receipt) of the IT Act are explained in point 6 below.
In simple words

Section 3: you communicate by any act or omission meant to communicate, or which actually communicates: words, a letter, an email, a nod, conduct. Section 4, offer: an offer is communicated only when the other person knows of it. Section 4, acceptance : there are two moments . The proposer is bound as soon as the acceptance is sent beyond the acceptor's control (posted). The acceptor is bound only when the acceptance reaches the proposer's knowledge . Section 4, revocation : the same two-moment pattern (details in the revocation topic). Section 5: the gap between those two moments is why a proposer can revoke until the acceptance is posted, and an acceptor can revoke his acceptance until it reaches the proposer. IT Act, Section 10A: a contract is not unenforceable merely because it was made by email or other electronic means. IT Act, Section 13: an email is sent when it leaves the sender's control, and received when it enters the receiver 's (designated) system; it is treated as sent from the sender's place of business and received at the receiver's place of business .
en.meaning:
What "communication" means

To communicate is to bring the offer or acceptance to the other side's notice. Under Section 3 it may be:

express : spoken words, a letter, a telegram, an email, an SMS; by conduct : an act that shows the intention, such as delivering goods or encashing a cheque .

Why the moment matters

The exact moment of communication decides:

when the contract is formed, and therefore when each party is bound; until when an offer or acceptance can be revoked (Section 5); and where the contract is made, which decides which court has jurisdiction .

Section 4 in a table

What is communicated Complete as against the sender Complete as against the receiver Proposal — (only one moment) When it comes to the receiver's knowledge Acceptance As against the acceptor : when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer As against the proposer : when it is put in a course of transmission to him Revocation When put into a course of transmission When it comes to the receiver's knowledge

Note the twist for acceptance: the proposer (the receiver of the acceptance) is bound earlier , at the moment of posting; the acceptor (the sender) is bound later , at the moment of receipt.

Running example

Meena lives in Hyderabad . Ravi lives in Vijayawada . Meena writes to Ravi offering to sell her sewing machine, model XL-200, for ₹8,000 .

Monday: Meena posts the offer. Wednesday: the letter reaches Ravi and he reads it. Thursday, 10 a.m.: Ravi posts his letter of acceptance. Saturday, 11 a.m.: Meena receives Ravi's letter.

We will use these dates throughout.
keyPoints: Communication can be by any act or omission meant to communicate (Section 3). An offer is communicated when it comes to the knowledge of the offeree (Section 4). Acceptance has two moments : against the proposer on posting ; against the acceptor on receipt (Section 4, ill. (b)). The proposer is bound first in the post; a lost letter of acceptance does not save him ( Household Fire ), unless he required actual notice ( Holwell ). For telephone and telex, the contract is made when and where the acceptance is received ( Entores ; Bhagwandas , majority; Hidayatullah J dissenting). Email contracts are valid ( Trimex ; IT Act, Section 10A); despatch and receipt are fixed by IT Act, Section 13. The place of contract gives a court jurisdiction .

caseLaws.name: Entores Ltd
caseLaws.facts: v. Miles Far East Corporation (1955) Facts. Entores in London and the Amsterdam agents of Miles Far East Corporation made a contract for copper cathodes by telex. The acceptance was sent from Amsterdam and received in London. Principle. For instantaneous communication, the contract is complete only when the acceptance is received by the offeror, and it is made where the acceptance is received. [1955] 2 QB 327 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It is the source of the instantaneous-communication rule followed in India. Bhagwandas Goverdhandas Kedia v. Girdharilal Parshottamdas & Co. (1965) Facts. An offer from Ahmedabad to buy cotton seed cake was accepted on the telephone at Khamgaon. The buyers sued at Ahmedabad; the sellers said the court had no jurisdiction. Principle. A contract by telephone is complete when and where the acceptance is heard by the proposer; the postal rule is an exception of convenience that does not apply to telephones (majority; Hidayatullah J dissenting). AIR 1966 SC 543 : (1966) 1 SCR 656. Why it matters. It is the leading Indian case on telephone contracts and the place of contract . Trimex International FZE Ltd. v. Vedanta Aluminium Ltd. (2010) Facts. An offer for supply of bauxite was made by email on 15 October 2007 and accepted by email on 16 October 2007 ("we confirm the deal for five shipments"). The formal contract was never signed. Principle. A contract concluded by email is binding; the acceptance is complete under Section 4 when it comes to the proposer's knowledge, and an unsigned formal contract does not undo it. Supreme Court, Arbitration Petition No. 10 of 2009, decided 22 January 2010. Why it matters. It is the leading Supreme Court case on contracts by email . Adams v. Lindsell (1818) Facts. An offer to sell wool, received on 5 September, was accepted by a letter posted the same day, which arrived on 9 September. The sellers had sold the wool to someone else on 8 September. Principle. A contract by post is complete when the letter of acceptance is posted. (1818) 1 B & Ald 681. Why it matters. It is the origin of the postal rule that Section 4 adopts as against the proposer. Household Fire and Carriage Accident Insurance Co. v. Grant (1879) Facts. A letter of allotment of shares was posted to Grant but never reached him. Principle. The contract was complete on posting, so Grant was bound even though the letter was lost. (1879) 4 Ex D 216. Why it matters. It shows the risk of loss in the post falls on the proposer. Holwell Securities Ltd. v. Hughes (1974) Facts. An option to buy property had to be exercised "by notice in writing" to the seller. The letter exercising it was posted but never arrived. Principle. Where the offer requires actual communication, the postal rule does not apply. [1974] 1 WLR 155. Why it matters. It shows the proposer can exclude the postal rule.

selfTest.q: 1. When is the communication of an offer complete?
selfTest.a: When it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made (Section 4, ill. (a)).

selfTest.q: 2. Ravi posts an acceptance on Thursday; it reaches Meena on Saturday. When is Meena bound, and when is Ravi bound?
selfTest.a: Meena on Thursday (on posting); Ravi on Saturday (on receipt) (Section 4, ill. (b)).

selfTest.q: 3. Can Meena revoke her offer on Friday?
selfTest.a: No. The acceptance was complete as against her on Thursday (Section 5).

selfTest.q: 4. Where is a contract made by telephone?
selfTest.a: Where the acceptance is heard by the proposer ( Bhagwandas , majority).

selfTest.q: 5. Who dissented in Bhagwandas , and why?
selfTest.a: Hidayatullah J, because the words of Section 4 cover the telephone, so the acceptance was complete where it was spoken.

selfTest.q: 6. Is a contract by email valid if the formal contract is never signed?
selfTest.a: Yes ( Trimex ; IT Act, Section 10A).

selfTest.q: 7. Where is an email deemed to be received?
selfTest.a: At the addressee's place of business (IT Act, Section 13(3)).

law-of-contract-i-u1-t5.subtitle: Sections 4 to 6 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872; sections 10A and 13 of the Information Technology Act, 2000

en.inOneMinute: Revocation means taking back an offer or an acceptance before it binds. Section 5 sets the deadline: a proposal can be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer (in the post, until the acceptance is posted), but not afterwards; an acceptance can be revoked at any time before the communication of the acceptance is complete as against the acceptor (in the post, until it reaches the proposer), but not afterwards. Section 6 lists the modes by which a proposal comes to an end: (1) notice of revocation , (2) lapse of time , (3) failure of a condition precedent , and (4) death or insanity of the proposer, if the acceptor learns of it before accepting. A rejection or counter-offer also ends an offer. A revocation must itself be communicated (Section 4). Revocation by email or other electronic means is valid (IT Act, Section 10A), and the IT Act fixes when an electronic revocation is sent and received (Section 13). In exams, marks come from Sections 5 and 6 quoted with the illustration, the timeline of when each party can revoke, cases such as Byrne v. Van Tienhoven , Dickinson v. Dodds and Shuey , and the electronic rules. In real life, it tells you how long you can change your mind.
legalProvision: Section 5. Revocation of proposals and acceptances. A proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer, but not afterwards. An acceptance may be revoked at any time before the communication of the acceptance is complete as against the acceptor, but not afterwards. Illustration A proposes, by a letter sent by post, to sell his house to B. B accepts the proposal by a letter sent by post. A may revoke his proposal at any time before or at the moment when B posts his letter of acceptance, but not afterwards. B may revoke his acceptance at any time before or at the moment when the letter communicating it reaches A, but not afterwards.

Section 5, Uttar Pradesh amendment (U.P. Act 57 of 1976). At the end of the first paragraph, the following Explanation is inserted: "Explanation—Where an invitation to a proposal contains a condition that any proposal made in response to such invitation shall be kept open for a specified time and a proposal is thereupon made accepting such condition, such proposal may not be revoked within such time."

Section 6. Revocation how made. A proposal is revoked— (1) by the communication of notice of revocation by the proposer to the other party; (2) by the lapse of the time prescribed in such proposal for its acceptance, or, if no time is so prescribed, by the lapse of a reasonable time, without communication of the acceptance; (3) by the failure of the acceptor to fulfil a condition precedent to acceptance; or (4) by the death or insanity of the proposer, if the fact of his death or insanity comes to the knowledge of the acceptor before acceptance.

Section 4 (third paragraph and illustration (c)). The communication of a revocation is complete,— as against the person who makes it, when it is put into a course of transmission to the person to whom it is made, so as to be out of the power of the person who makes it; as against the person to whom it is made, when it comes to his knowledge. (c) A revokes his proposal by telegram. The revocation is complete as against A when the telegram is despatched. It is complete as against B when B receives it. B revokes his acceptance by telegram. B's revocation is complete as against B when the telegram is despatched, and as against A when it reaches him.

Section 3 (relevant part). … the revocation of proposals and acceptances, respectively, are deemed to be made by any act or omission of the party … revoking by which he intends to communicate such … revocation, or which has the effect of communicating it.
Information Technology Act, 2000

Section 10A. Validity of contracts formed through electronic means. Where in a contract formation, the communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, the revocation of proposals and acceptances, as the case may be, are expressed in electronic form or by means of an electronic records, such contract shall not be deemed to be unenforceable solely on the ground that such electronic form or means was used for that purpose.

Section 13(1). Save as otherwise agreed to between the originator and the addressee, the despatch of an electronic record occurs when it enters a computer resource outside the control of the originator.
Section 13(2) to (5) (time and place of receipt), Section 11 (attribution), Section 12 (acknowledgment) and the First Schedule are explained in point 9 below.
In simple words

Section 5: the proposer can take back his offer until the acceptance is sent beyond the acceptor's control . The acceptor can take back his acceptance until it reaches the proposer . UP amendment: in Uttar Pradesh, if a tender notice says offers must stay open for a fixed time, and you make an offer on that condition, you cannot withdraw it within that time. Section 6: an offer ends by (1) notice of revocation, (2) time running out , (3) the acceptor not fulfilling a condition that had to be met before accepting, or (4) the proposer's death or insanity , if the acceptor knew of it before accepting. Section 4: a revocation is complete against the person revoking when he sends it; against the other side when it reaches his knowledge . IT Act, Section 10A: a revocation by email or electronic means is as good as one on paper. IT Act, Section 13(1): an email is sent when it leaves the sender's control.
en.meaning:
What revocation means

Revocation is the withdrawal of a proposal or an acceptance by the person who made it, before it becomes binding. It is different from:

rejection , which is the offeree saying "no" to the offer; and lapse , where the offer ends without anyone acting, because time runs out.

Why the law allows revocation

An offer is only a proposal. Until it is accepted, there is no promise, so the proposer is free to withdraw. An acceptance by post binds the proposer when posted, but the acceptor is bound only when it arrives. The Act lets the acceptor withdraw during that gap, so that both sides have some protection.

The revocation windows in one table

Who revokes What Deadline (Section 5) In the post Proposer His proposal Before acceptance is complete as against the proposer Until the acceptance is posted Acceptor His acceptance Before acceptance is complete as against the acceptor Until the acceptance reaches the proposer

Running example

Meena (Hyderabad) offers by post to sell her sewing machine, model XL-200, to Ravi (Vijayawada) for ₹8,000 , "open till Friday".

Monday: Meena posts the offer. Wednesday: Ravi reads it. Thursday, 10 a.m.: Ravi posts his letter of acceptance. Saturday, 11 a.m.: Meena receives Ravi's letter.
keyPoints: Proposer may revoke until the acceptance is complete as against him (in the post: until it is posted ) (Section 5). Acceptor may revoke until the acceptance is complete as against him (in the post: until it reaches the proposer) (Section 5). Revocation must be communicated (Section 4; Byrne ). Modes: notice, lapse, failure of condition precedent, death or insanity known before acceptance (Section 6). A promise to keep an offer open is not binding without consideration ( Routledge v. Grant ), except under the UP amendment for tender-type proposals. A general offer is revoked by the same publicity ( Shuey ). Electronic revocation is valid (IT Act, Section 10A); its despatch and receipt are fixed by Section 13. The IT Act does not apply to certain negotiable instruments, powers of attorney, trusts and wills (First Schedule); the immovable-property entry was omitted in 2022.

caseLaws.name: Byrne & Co
caseLaws.facts: v. Van Tienhoven & Co. (1880) Facts. An offer posted on 1 October was received and accepted by telegram on 11 October. A letter of revocation posted on 8 October reached the offerees on 20 October. Principle. A revocation has no effect until it is communicated to the offeree; an acceptance made before then binds. (1880) 5 CPD 344. Why it matters. It shows that posting a revocation is not enough; it must reach the offeree (as in Section 4). Dickinson v. Dodds (1876) Facts. Dodds offered to sell houses to Dickinson for £800, open until 9 a.m. on Friday, 12 June 1874. He sold them to another person before then, and Dickinson learned of it through Berry. Principle. A promise to keep an offer open is not binding without consideration, and an offeree who knows from a reliable source that the property has been sold cannot then accept. (1876) 2 Ch D 463. Why it matters. It shows revocation can be communicated indirectly , and that firm offers without consideration can be withdrawn. Routledge v. Grant (1828) Facts. The defendant offered to buy a house, giving six weeks for an answer, and withdrew before the six weeks ended. Principle. An offer may be withdrawn before acceptance even if a time was fixed for acceptance, where there is no consideration for keeping it open. (1828) 4 Bing 653. Why it matters. It explains why Section 5 lets the proposer revoke "at any time" before acceptance. Shuey v. United States (1875) Facts. A $25,000 reward for the arrest of John H. Surratt, offered by public proclamation on 20 April 1865, was revoked by a proclamation published the same way on 24 November 1865. Information was later given by a man who did not know of the revocation. Principle. A general offer may be revoked through the same channel by which it was made, even if a particular person does not learn of the revocation. 92 US 73 (1875). Why it matters. It shows how a general offer is revoked. Payne v. Cave (1789) Facts. A bidder at an auction withdrew his bid before the auctioneer's hammer fell. Principle. A bid is an offer, which may be withdrawn before it is accepted by the fall of the hammer. (1789) 3 TR 148. Why it matters. It applies the revocation rule to auctions . Hyde v. Wrench (1840) Facts. Hyde offered £950 against Wrench's offer to sell at £1,000, and later tried to accept the £1,000 offer. Principle. A counter-offer rejects the original offer, which then ends. (1840) 49 ER 132. Why it matters. It shows that an offer also ends by rejection , apart from the modes in Section 6.

selfTest.q: 1. Until when can a proposer revoke an offer, when acceptance is by post?
selfTest.a: Until the letter of acceptance is posted (Section 5, illustration).

selfTest.q: 2. Until when can the acceptor revoke his acceptance by post?
selfTest.a: Until the letter of acceptance reaches the proposer (Section 5, illustration).

selfTest.q: 3. Is a revocation effective when posted?
selfTest.a: Only as against the person revoking. As against the other party, only when it comes to his knowledge (Section 4; Byrne v. Van Tienhoven ).

selfTest.q: 5. Is a promise to keep an offer open for a week binding?
selfTest.a: Not without consideration ( Routledge v. Grant ), except under the UP amendment where a proposal is made accepting a "keep open" condition in an invitation.

selfTest.q: 6. Is a revocation by email valid?
selfTest.a: Yes (IT Act, Section 10A).

selfTest.q: 7. When is an email revocation sent?
selfTest.a: When it enters a computer resource outside the sender's control (IT Act, Section 13(1)).

law-of-contract-i-u1-t10.subtitle: Trusts, family arrangements, agency, assignment, estoppel, covenants running with land and statutes

en.inOneMinute: The general rule of privity is that only a party to a contract can sue on it ( Dunlop v. Selfridge ; M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore ). But the rule would cause injustice in some cases, so the courts recognise exceptions in which a person who is not a party can enforce the contract, or is treated as a party: Trust or charge : a beneficiary under a trust, or a person in whose favour a charge on property is created by the contract ( Khwaja Muhammad Khan v. Husaini Begam ). Marriage settlement, partition or other family arrangement , where provision is made for a family member ( M.C. Chacko recognises this exception). Acknowledgment or estoppel : where the promisor, by his conduct or acknowledgment, makes himself directly liable to the third person ( Narayani Devi v. Tagore Commercial Corporation ). Assignment : the benefit of a contract can be assigned, and the assignee can enforce it. Agency : a principal can sue and be sued on a contract made by his agent (Sections 182, 226, 230). Covenants running with land : a purchaser of land with notice of a restrictive covenant can be bound by it ( Tulk v. Moxhay ). In exams, marks come from stating the rule first, then each exception with its basis and a case. In real life, it tells a widow, a family member, a buyer of a debt or a principal when they can sue on a contract they did not sign.
legalProvision: There is no single section listing the exceptions. They come from case law and from the provisions below.
Section 2(c). The person making the proposal is called the "promisor", and the person accepting the proposal is called the "promisee";

Section 2(d). When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise;

Section 182. "Agent" and "principal" defined. An "agent" is a person employed to do any act for another, or to represent another in dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the "principal".

Section 226. Enforcement and consequences of agent's contracts. Contracts entered into through an agent, and obligations arising from acts done by an agent, may be enforced in the same manner, and will have the same legal consequences, as if the contracts had been entered into and the acts done by the principal in person.

Section 230 (first paragraph). In the absence of any contract to that effect, an agent cannot personally enforce contracts entered into by him on behalf of his principal, nor is he personally bound by them.

The rule and its exceptions, in the words of the Supreme Court ( M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore , 1969): "It must therefore be taken as well settled that except in the case of a beneficiary under a trust created by a contract or in the case of a family arrangement, no right may be enforced by a person who is not a party to the contract."
In simple words

Sections 2(c), 2(d): the parties are the promisor and promisee; consideration may come from anyone. The privity rule comes from these definitions. Section 182: an agent acts for a principal . Section 226: a contract made through an agent is enforced as if the principal made it himself . So the principal, who did not sign, can sue and be sued. Section 230: the agent normally cannot sue or be sued on it. M.C. Chacko: the Supreme Court named two exceptions expressly: a beneficiary under a trust and a family arrangement . Other exceptions come from other cases and statutes.
en.meaning:
What an "exception to privity" is

An exception is a situation in which a person who is not the promisee can still enforce a promise, or is bound by it, because the law treats him as having a direct right or duty.

Why the exceptions exist

Justice to the intended beneficiary. Where the whole purpose of the contract is to provide for a person, such as a wife or a widow, it would be unjust to leave her without a remedy. Equity. A trust or charge gives the beneficiary an equitable right, not a contractual one. In M.C. Chacko , the Supreme Court explained that a beneficiary under a trust may enforce the rights the trust gives him because "though he is not a party to the contract his rights are equitable and not contractual." Representation. In agency, the principal is the real party; the agent is only his instrument. Commercial need. Debts and other contract rights must be transferable ( assignment ).

Running example (the rule)

Kavya sells her car to Madhu for ₹4,00,000 , and Madhu promises Kavya to pay ₹1,00,000 of the price directly to Kavya's creditor Suresh . Madhu does not pay. Under the rule, Suresh cannot sue Madhu ( M.C. Chacko ; Jamna Das v. Ram Autar ). Below, we change the facts to fit each exception.
keyPoints: The rule: only parties can sue ( Dunlop ; M.C. Chacko ). Trust or charge : beneficiary can enforce in equity ( Khwaja Muhammad Khan ). Family arrangement , marriage settlement or partition: family member provided for can enforce ( M.C. Chacko ). Acknowledgment or estoppel : promisor's conduct creates direct liability ( Narayani Devi ). Assignment : benefit, not burden, can be transferred (Transfer of Property Act, Section 130). Agency : principal sues and is sued (Section 226); agent normally not (Section 230). Covenants running with land : purchaser with notice bound ( Tulk v. Moxhay ). Chinnaya v. Ramayya is about consideration, not an exception to privity.

caseLaws.name: Khwaja Muhammad Khan v
caseLaws.facts: Husaini Begam (1910) Facts. Before the marriage of two minors in 1877, the bridegroom's father agreed with the bride's father to pay the bride Rs. 500 a month in perpetuity, charged on immovable property. The wife later sued for arrears. Principle. "although no party to the document, she is clearly entitled to proceed in equity to enforce her claim." (1910) 37 IA 152 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It is the leading case on the trust or charge and marriage settlement exceptions. M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore (1969) Facts. A father's family deed directed his son to pay any amount due to a bank under the father's guarantee. The bank sued to enforce the deed against the son and his properties. Principle. A non-party cannot enforce a contract "except in the case of a beneficiary under a trust created by a contract or in the case of a family arrangement"; the bank was neither. AIR 1970 SC 500 : (1969) 2 SCC 343. Why it matters. It states the rule and the two main exceptions for India, and shows their limits. Narayani Devi v. Tagore Commercial Corporation Ltd. (1972) Facts. A company agreed with a husband, who transferred shares to it, to pay Rs. 250 a month to his widow after his death. After he died, the widow sued for arrears. Principle. The company's acknowledgment and conduct towards the widow created privity, and she could recover. AIR 1973 Cal 401 (Calcutta High Court). Why it matters. It illustrates the acknowledgment or estoppel exception. Tulk v. Moxhay (1848) Facts. Land in Leicester Square was sold subject to a covenant to keep it as a garden. A later purchaser, Moxhay, who knew of the covenant, wanted to build on it. Principle. A purchaser with notice of a restrictive covenant is bound by it in equity and can be restrained by injunction. (1848) 41 ER 1143. Why it matters. It is the leading case on covenants running with land .

selfTest.a: A beneficiary under a trust created by a contract, and a family arrangement.

selfTest.q: 2. Why could the wife sue in Khwaja Muhammad Khan?
selfTest.a: The allowance was charged on property for her benefit, so she could proceed in equity, though not a party.

selfTest.q: 3. Why did the bank lose in M.C. Chacko?
selfTest.a: It was not a party, and the deed created no trust or charge in its favour.

selfTest.q: 4. Can the burden of a contract be assigned?
selfTest.a: Not without the other party's consent; only the benefit can be assigned.

selfTest.q: 5. Under which section is a contract made by an agent enforced as if made by the principal?
selfTest.a: Section 226.

selfTest.q: 6. Which case is the authority for covenants running with land?
selfTest.a: Tulk v. Moxhay (1848).

law-of-contract-i-u1-t7.subtitle: Sections 2(d), 23 and 25 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A promise is enforced by law only when something is given in return for it. That "something in return" is consideration . It is the price of the promise . Under Section 2(d), consideration is an act, abstinence or promise , done at the desire of the promisor , by the promisee or any other person . It may be past, present or future . It need not be adequate , but it must be real and lawful . Without it, an agreement is void (Section 25), except in a few cases. Indian law is wider than English law on two points: who may give consideration, and past consideration. This is a favourite long-answer topic. In real life, it explains why a gift promise cannot be enforced but a sale can.
legalProvision: Section 2(d). When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise.
Section 2(f). Promises which form the consideration or part of the consideration for each other are called reciprocal promises.

Section 10 (relevant part). All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.

Section 23 (opening words). The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful, unless it is forbidden by law; or is of such a nature that, if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law; or is fraudulent; or involves or implies injury to the person or property of another; or the Court regards it as immoral, or opposed to public policy.
Section 25 (opening words). An agreement made without consideration is void, unless … (the three exceptions are in the note Exception to consideration ).

Section 25, Explanation 2. An agreement to which the consent of the promisor is freely given is not void merely because the consideration is inadequate; but the inadequacy of the consideration may be taken into account by the Court in determining the question whether the consent of the promisor was freely given.
In simple words

Section 2(d) says what consideration is. Section 2(f) says that two promises given for each other are reciprocal promises . Section 10 says a valid contract needs lawful consideration . Section 23 says when consideration is unlawful . Section 25 says an agreement without consideration is void , except in a few cases. Its Explanation 2 says a small consideration is still consideration.
en.meaning:
The idea: something for something Consideration is what each side gives or promises in exchange for the other's promise. The Latin phrase is quid pro quo , "something for something". The law enforces bargains , not bare promises. A bare promise without consideration is a nudum pactum (a naked promise). The maxim ex nudo pacto non oritur actio means no action arises from a bare promise . Why the law asks for consideration. It separates a bargain from a gift. In a bargain, each side has given or risked something, so it is fair to enforce it. A bare promise to give a gift has nothing behind it. The classic English definition In Currie v. Misa (1875), consideration was described as some right, interest, profit or benefit to one party, or some forbearance, detriment, loss or responsibility given, suffered or undertaken by the other. Put simply, it is either a benefit to the promisor or a detriment (loss or burden) to the promisee. The Indian definition, broken into parts Read Section 2(d) as five questions. Part of Section 2(d) Question to ask Answer in simple words "at the desire of the promisor" Who asked for it? The promisor must have wanted it "the promisee or any other person" Who gave it? The promisee, or even a third person "has done … does … promises to do" When was it given? Past, present or future "done or abstained from doing" What kind of thing? An act, an abstinence, or a promise "something" How much ? Anything of some value in law, even if small Running example Ravi promises to pay Sita ₹15,000 for her used scooter. Sita promises to hand over the scooter next Sunday. Ravi is the promisor of the promise to pay. Sita is the promisee . Sita's promise to hand over the scooter is the consideration for Ravi's promise. Ravi's promise to pay ₹15,000 is the consideration for Sita's promise. Each promise is the price of the other. These are reciprocal promises (Section 2(f)). See Diagram 1 (when consideration is given: past, present, future). Diagram 1. Section 2(d): "has done", "does", "promises to do". flowchart LR P["PAST · 'has done'

Past: done before the promise, at the promisor's request (Bala repairs Arjun's tractor in March; Arjun promises ₹4,000 in May). Present, executed: given at the same time (Ravi pays ₹15,000 and takes the scooter). Future, executory: to be given later (both promise to perform on Sunday).
keyPoints: Consideration is the price of the promise : something for something. Section 2(d): an act, abstinence or promise , done at the desire of the promisor , by the promisee or any other person . It may be past, present or future . It need not be adequate (Section 25, Explanation 2), but inadequacy may show that consent was not free. It must be real (not impossible, uncertain, or an existing duty) and lawful (Sections 10, 23). Promises given for each other are reciprocal promises (Section 2(f)). Consideration need not be money. Motive is not consideration. Indian law is wider than English law on third-party and past consideration. An agreement without consideration is void , except in the Section 25 cases.

caseLaws.name: Durga Prasad v
caseLaws.facts: Baldeo (1880) Facts. Durga Prasad built shops in a market at Etawah at the Collector's request. The shopkeepers who occupied them signed an agreement to pay him a commission on goods sold there. Principle. An act done at the desire of a third person, not the promisor, is not consideration. Nor was it done "for the promisor" under Section 25(2). (1881) ILR 3 All 221. Why it matters. It is the leading Indian case on "at the desire of the promisor". Chinnaya v. Ramayya (1882) Facts. An old lady gifted her property to her daughter on condition that the daughter pay an annuity to the old lady's sister. The daughter promised but did not pay. Principle. Under Section 2(d), consideration may move from "any other person". The sister could recover. ILR (1882) 4 Mad 137. Why it matters. It shows that Indian law is wider than English law on who may give consideration. Sindha Shri Ganpatsingji v. Abraham (1895) Facts. Services were done for the defendant at his request. He later promised to pay for them. Principle. Past services done at the promisor's request are good consideration for a later promise. ILR (1895) 20 Bom 755. Why it matters. It confirms that past consideration is valid in India. Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt (1913) Facts. A servant was already sent to search for his master's missing nephew. He found the boy and claimed a reward announced after he had left. Principle. Doing what one is already bound to do is not fresh consideration. Allahabad High Court, 1913. Why it matters. It applies the existing-duty rule in India. It is also studied under acceptance (knowledge of the offer). Thomas v. Thomas (1842) Facts. Executors let a widow live in her late husband's house for life at a rent of £1 a year. Principle. Consideration need not be adequate, and motive is not consideration. (1842) 2 QB 851. Why it matters. It supports the inadequacy rule in Section 25, Explanation 2. Currie v. Misa (1875) Facts. A dispute over a cheque given to a bank for an existing debt. Principle. Consideration is some benefit to one party or some detriment to the other. (1875) LR 10 Ex 153. Why it matters. It gives the classic definition of consideration. Tweddle v. Atkinson (1861) Facts. After the plaintiff's marriage, his father and his father-in-law agreed in writing to pay him £100 and £200. The father-in-law died without paying, and the plaintiff sued his executor. Principle. In English law, consideration must move from the promisee. The plaintiff gave none and could not sue. 121 ER 762. Why it matters. It marks the English rule that Indian law does not follow on this point.

selfTest.a: No. The work was not done at C's desire (Section 2(d); Durga Prasad v. Baldeo ).

selfTest.q: 2. Which words of Section 2(d) allow a third party to give consideration?
selfTest.a: "The promisee or any other person".

selfTest.q: 3. A freely agrees to sell a Rs. 1,000 horse for Rs. 10. Is it a contract?
selfTest.a: Yes. Inadequacy alone does not make it void (Section 25, Explanation 2 and illustration (f)).

selfTest.q: 4. Is past consideration valid in India?
selfTest.a: Yes, if the past act was done at the promisor's desire ( Sindha Shri Ganpatsingji v. Abraham ).

selfTest.q: 5. A police officer is promised ₹1,000 to investigate a theft he is already assigned to. Is there consideration?
selfTest.a: No. Performing an existing legal duty is not fresh consideration.

selfTest.q: 6. What are reciprocal promises?
selfTest.a: Promises which form the consideration, or part of it, for each other (Section 2(f)).

law-of-contract-i-u1-t6.subtitle: Articles 298 and 299 of the Constitution of India; section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Union and the States can make contracts like anyone else (Article 298), and can sue and be sued on them (Article 300). The Indian Contract Act applies to these contracts. But the Constitution adds formalities in Article 299(1) : a contract made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or a State must be expressed to be made by the President or the Governor , and executed on his behalf by such persons and in such manner as he directs or authorises . These formalities are mandatory . A contract that does not follow them is void and cannot be enforced by either side; there can be no implied contract with the Government, and no ratification or estoppel can cure the defect ( K.P. Chowdhary ; Mulamchand ). But if the Government has enjoyed the benefit of goods or work, it must pay compensation under Section 70 ( State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal ). Neither the President, the Governor nor the officer who signs is personally liable (Article 299(2)). When awarding contracts, the State must act fairly and non-arbitrarily (Article 14; Ramana Dayaram Shetty ; Kasturi Lal ). In exams, marks come from Article 299 quoted and broken into its three requirements, the effect of non-compliance with cases, the Section 70 remedy, and Article 14. In real life, it tells a supplier or contractor how to make sure a government order is binding.
legalProvision: Constitution of India

Article 298. Power to carry on trade, etc. The executive power of the Union and of each State shall extend to the carrying on of any trade or business and to the acquisition, holding and disposal of property and the making of contracts for any purpose: Provided that— (a) the said executive power of the Union shall, in so far as such trade or business or such purpose is not one with respect to which Parliament may make laws, be subject in each State to legislation by the State; and (b) the said executive power of each State shall, in so far as such trade or business or such purpose is not one with respect to which the State Legislature may make laws, be subject to legislation by Parliament.

Article 299. Contracts. (1) All contracts made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State shall be expressed to be made by the President, or by the Governor of the State, as the case may be, and all such contracts and all assurances of property made in the exercise of that power shall be executed on behalf of the President or the Governor by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise. (2) Neither the President nor the Governor shall be personally liable in respect of any contract or assurance made or executed for the purposes of this Constitution, or for the purposes of any enactment relating to the Government of India heretofore in force, nor shall any person making or executing any such contract or assurance on behalf of any of them be personally liable in respect thereof.

Article 300(1). Suits and proceedings. The Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India and the Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State and may, subject to any provisions which may be made by Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of such State enacted by virtue of powers conferred by this Constitution, sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces or the corresponding Indian States might have sued or been sued if this Constitution had not been enacted.
Indian Contract Act, 1872

Section 70. Obligation of person enjoying benefit of non-gratuitous act. Where a person lawfully does anything for another person, or delivers anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make compensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered.

Section 65. Obligation of person who has received advantage under void agreement, or contract that becomes void. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it.

Section 230 (relevant part). In the absence of any contract to that effect, an agent cannot personally enforce contracts entered into by him on behalf of his principal, nor is he personally bound by them. … Such a contract shall be presumed to exist in the following cases:— … (3) where the principal, though disclosed, cannot be sued.
In simple words

Article 298: the Government can do business, deal in property and make contracts for any purpose. Article 299(1): a government contract must say it is made by the President (or the Governor) and must be signed on his behalf by an authorised officer in the authorised manner . Article 299(2): the President, the Governor and the officer who signs are not personally liable on such contracts. Article 300: the Union is sued as " Union of India ", and a State by its name (for example, "State of Andhra Pradesh"). Section 70: if you lawfully do work or deliver goods to someone, not as a gift, and he enjoys the benefit , he must pay for it or return it , even without a valid contract. Section 65: a person who received an advantage under an agreement found to be void must restore it or pay for it. Section 230: an agent is normally not personally bound, but is presumed bound where his principal cannot be sued .
en.meaning:
What a government contract is

A government contract is a contract made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State, for example: buying supplies, awarding construction works, leasing government land, selling forest produce, or granting licences by auction.

Why the Constitution adds formalities

Public money is at stake. The formalities make sure that only authorised officers bind the Government, and only in the authorised manner. Certainty. It must be clear that the contract is the Government's, not the officer's private deal. Protection of the public interest. The Supreme Court has said the provisions are mandatory and "enacted in the public interest" ( Seth Bikhraj Jaipuria ).

Article 299(1) broken into parts

Requirement What it means Example "expressed to be made by the President, or by the Governor" The contract must say it is made in the name of the President or the Governor "This agreement is made by the Governor of Andhra Pradesh …" "executed on behalf of the President or the Governor" It must be signed on his behalf "For and on behalf of the Governor of Andhra Pradesh" "by such persons … as he may direct or authorise" The signing officer must be authorised (usually by a notification or rules of business) The District Collector, if authorised for such contracts "in such manner as he may direct or authorise" The authorised form must be followed A written deed in the authorised form

Because the contract must be "expressed" to be made and "executed", the Supreme Court has held that there can be no implied contract with the Government ( K.P. Chowdhary v. State of M.P. ).

Which contracts are covered

Article 299 covers contracts made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State . A company or corporation set up by the Government that contracts in its own name is a separate legal person; on the words of the Article, such a contract is not one made "in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State".

Running example

The District Collector, Krishna (Andhra Pradesh), wants 500 school desks. Ravi Furniture quotes ₹2,500 a desk, total ₹12,50,000 (500 × ₹2,500). We will test three versions of the deal:

Version A: a written agreement "made by the Governor of Andhra Pradesh", signed "for and on behalf of the Governor" by the Collector, who is authorised by notification to sign such contracts. Version B: the Collector simply writes a letter in his own name: "Supply 500 desks at ₹2,500 each." Version C: the same as Version B, and Ravi Furniture delivers all 500 desks, which the schools start using.
keyPoints: The Government can contract for any purpose (Article 298) and sue or be sued (Article 300). Article 299(1): in the name of the President or Governor, executed on his behalf, by an authorised person in the authorised manner . The formalities are mandatory ( Bikhraj Jaipuria ); there is no implied contract ( K.P. Chowdhary ). A non-complying contract is void ; no ratification or estoppel ( Mulamchand ). The Government must pay for benefits it enjoys under Section 70 ( B.K. Mondal ). No personal liability of the President, Governor or signing officer (Article 299(2)). A valid government contract is enforced on its terms ( Alopi Parshad ). The State must not act arbitrarily in awarding contracts (Article 14; Ramana Dayaram Shetty ; Kasturi Lal ).

caseLaws.name: State of West Bengal v
caseLaws.facts: B.K. Mondal & Sons (1961) Facts. Contractors built structures at Arambagh and Khanakul in 1944 for the Civil Supplies Department under contracts that did not follow the required form. They sued for Rs. 19,325. Principle. A non-complying contract is invalid, but the State must pay under Section 70 for work lawfully done, not gratuitously, whose benefit it enjoyed. AIR 1962 SC 779 : 1962 Supp (1) SCR 876. Why it matters. It is the leading case on the Section 70 remedy against the Government. Seth Bikhraj Jaipuria v. Union of India (1961) Facts. A railway officer placed orders for foodgrains in 1943 that were not made in the name of the Governor-General. The Railway stopped accepting deliveries, and the supplier sued. Principle. The formalities are mandatory and "enacted in the public interest"; a contract not complying with them does not bind the Government. AIR 1962 SC 113 : (1962) 2 SCR 880. Why it matters. It establishes that the formalities are mandatory . K.P. Chowdhary v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1966) Facts. The highest bidder at a 1959 forest auction refused to complete; no written contract had been executed. The State re-auctioned and tried to recover the deficiency of Rs. 51,500 from him. Principle. "in view of Art. 299(1) there can be no implied contract between the Government and another person"; the State could not recover. AIR 1967 SC 203 : (1966) 3 SCR 919. Why it matters. It shows non-compliance binds neither side. Mulamchand v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1968) Facts. A contract for forest produce with the Deputy Commissioner did not comply with Article 299(1). The contractor sought a refund of his deposit of Rs. 10,000. Principle. The provisions are mandatory; "There is no question of estoppel or ratification in such a case"; Section 70 may apply, but the claimant must account for the benefit he received. AIR 1968 SC 1218 : (1968) 3 SCR 214. Why it matters. It settles that there is no ratification or estoppel . Chatturbhuj Vithaldas Jasani v. Moreshwar Parashram (1954) Facts. Contracts to supply bidis to the Government were not made in the form required by Article 299(1). Principle. The Court said such contracts were "not void simply because the Union Government could not have been sued on them by reason of article 299(1)" and could be ratified. AIR 1954 SC 236 : 1954 SCR 817. Why it matters. It is the earlier view , later not followed on ratification ( Mulamchand ). Alopi Parshad & Sons Ltd. v. Union of India (1960) Facts. Agents appointed by agreement with the Governor-General to supply ghee to the Army from 1937 claimed higher rates when wartime costs rose. Principle. A contract is not frustrated merely because circumstances change, and quantum meruit cannot be awarded where the contract fixes the price. Supreme Court, decided 20 January 1960, (1960) 2 SCR 793. Why it matters. It shows a valid government contract is enforced on its terms , like any other contract. Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India (1979) Facts. A tender for a restaurant at Bombay airport was awarded to a person who did not meet the eligibility condition in the tender notice. Principle. The State must act according to a standard that is not arbitrary, irrational or irrelevant; departure from its own conditions violated Article 14. AIR 1979 SC 1628 : (1979) 3 SCC 489. Why it matters. It brings Article 14 into the award of government contracts.

selfTest.a: Expressed to be made by the President or Governor; executed on his behalf; by a person and in a manner he directs or authorises.

selfTest.q: 2. Can there be an oral or implied contract with the Government?
selfTest.a: No ( K.P. Chowdhary v. State of M.P. ).

selfTest.q: 3. Can the Government ratify a contract that does not comply with Article 299(1)?
selfTest.a: No. "There is no question of estoppel or ratification in such a case" ( Mulamchand ).

selfTest.q: 4. A contractor builds a structure for the State without a valid contract, and the State uses it. Can he recover anything?
selfTest.a: Yes, compensation under Section 70 ( State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal ).

selfTest.q: 5. Is the officer who signs a government contract personally liable?
selfTest.a: No, for a contract made in the required form (Article 299(2)).

selfTest.q: 6. In whose name is a State Government sued?
selfTest.a: In the name of the State (Article 300(1)).

selfTest.q: 7. Which Article limits the State's choice in awarding contracts?
selfTest.a: Article 14 ( Ramana Dayaram Shetty ; Kasturi Lal ).
