law-of-contract-i-u1-t9.subtitle: Section 2(d) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 and the common law rule that only parties can sue

en.inOneMinute: The doctrine of privity of contract says that only the parties to a contract can sue on it , and only they can be sued on it. A person who is not a party, a "third party" or "stranger", has no right to enforce the contract, even if it was made for his benefit. The Indian Contract Act does not state the rule in one section, but it follows from the definitions: the promisor is the person making the proposal and the promisee is the person accepting it (Section 2(c)), and Section 37 says "the parties to a contract" must perform their promises. The Supreme Court confirmed the rule in M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore (1969), following Dunlop v. Selfridge and Jamna Das v. Ram Autar . Keep two ideas apart: privity of contract (who is a party?) applies in India; but privity of consideration (must consideration come from the plaintiff?) does not , because Section 2(d) allows consideration to move from "the promisee or any other person ". There are recognised exceptions (trust or charge, family arrangement, acknowledgment, agency, assignment , covenants running with land). They are covered in Exceptions to the privity of contract . In exams, marks come from the meaning, the statutory basis, the two aspects of privity, Tweddle , Dunlop and M.C. Chacko , and a short note on exceptions. In real life, it tells you whether you can sue on a contract you did not sign.
legalProvision: Section 2(b). When the person to whom the proposal is made signifies his assent thereto, the proposal is said to be accepted. A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise;
Section 2(c). The person making the proposal is called the "promisor", and the person accepting the proposal is called the "promisee";

Section 2(d). When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise;
Section 2(e). Every promise and every set of promises, forming the consideration for each other, is an agreement;
Section 2(h). An agreement enforceable by law is a contract;

Section 37 (first paragraph). Obligation of parties to contracts. The parties to a contract must either perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the provisions of this Act, or of any other law.
In simple words

Section 2(c): the promisor is the one who makes the proposal; the promisee is the one who accepts it. These two are the parties . Section 2(d): the consideration may be given by the promisee or by someone else . Sections 2(e), 2(h): promises exchanged between the parties form an agreement; if enforceable, a contract . Section 37: it is the parties who must perform; the duty and the right lie between them. Read together, these sections make the contract a link between the parties . A third person is outside that link.
en.meaning:
What "privity" means

"Privity" means a relationship that exists between the parties to a transaction. Privity of contract is the relationship between the parties to a contract. The doctrine of privity draws two consequences from it:

A stranger to a contract cannot sue on it , even if the contract was made for his benefit. A stranger to a contract cannot be sued on it : the parties cannot impose duties on a person who did not agree.

The two aspects of privity

Aspect Question English law Indian law Privity of contract Is the plaintiff a party to the contract? Only a party can sue ( Dunlop ) Only a party can sue ( M.C. Chacko ; Jamna Das ) Privity of consideration Did the consideration move from the plaintiff? It must ( Tweddle ; Dunlop ) Not needed: "the promisee or any other person" (Section 2(d))

So in India a promisee can sue even if a third person gave the consideration; but a third person who is not a promisee cannot sue, even if he gave consideration or was meant to benefit. The Calcutta High Court explained this in Krishna Lal Sadhu v. Pramila Bala Dasi (Rankin CJ), quoted with approval by the Supreme Court in M.C. Chacko : Section 2(d) widens consideration, but "there is nothing in s. 2 to encourage the idea that contracts can be enforced by a person who is not a party to the contract, but this notion is rightly excluded by the definition of 'promisor' and 'promisee'."

Why the law has this rule

Freedom of contract. The parties chose each other. A stranger should not be able to step in and enforce, or be burdened by, a bargain he did not make. Mutuality. In Tweddle v. Atkinson , Crompton J said it would be "a monstrous proposition to say that a person was a party to the contract for the purpose of suing upon it for his own advantage, and not a party to it for the purpose of being sued." Freedom to vary. The parties may wish to change or cancel their contract. If third parties had rights, they could not do so freely.

Running example

Kavya sells her car to Madhu for ₹4,00,000 . As part of the price, Madhu promises Kavya that he will pay ₹1,00,000 directly to Suresh , to whom Kavya owes money, and pay the balance of ₹3,00,000 to Kavya (₹1,00,000 + ₹3,00,000 = ₹4,00,000). Madhu pays Kavya ₹3,00,000 but never pays Suresh.

Parties: Kavya (promisee of Madhu's promise to pay) and Madhu (promisor). Third party: Suresh, who benefits from the promise but did not make or accept it.
keyPoints: Only parties to a contract can sue or be sued on it. Statutory basis: promisor and promisee are the parties (Section 2(c)); parties must perform (Section 37). Tweddle v. Atkinson (1861): stranger to consideration cannot sue. Dunlop v. Selfridge (1915): "only a person who is a party to a contract can sue on it." M.C. Chacko (1969): rule applies in India, except a beneficiary under a trust or a family arrangement. Privity of consideration does not apply in India (Section 2(d)); privity of contract does. The promisee can sue even if the benefit was for a third person. Exceptions: trust/charge, family arrangement, acknowledgment, assignment, agency, covenants running with land.

caseLaws.name: Tweddle v
caseLaws.facts: Atkinson (1861) Facts. The fathers of a newly married couple agreed in writing that each would pay a sum to the bridegroom, who was given "full power to sue". The bride's father died without paying, and the bridegroom sued his executor. Principle. "no stranger to the consideration can take advantage of a contract, although made for his benefit." (1861) 121 ER 762 (Queen's Bench). Why it matters. It is the starting point of the privity doctrine in English law. Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co. Ltd. v. Selfridge & Co. Ltd. (1915) Facts. Selfridge promised Dew & Co. not to sell Dunlop tyres below list price and to pay Dunlop £5 per tyre for any breach. Selfridge sold below list price, and Dunlop sued. Principle. "only a person who is a party to a contract can sue on it. Our law knows nothing of a jus quaesitum tertio arising by way of contract." [1915] AC 847 (House of Lords). Why it matters. It is the classic statement of the privity rule . M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore (1969) Facts. A father's family deed said his son would pay any amount due to a bank under the father's guarantee. The bank sued the son and his properties under the deed. Principle. A person not a party to a contract cannot enforce it, except a beneficiary under a trust created by the contract or in the case of a family arrangement. AIR 1970 SC 500 : (1969) 2 SCC 343. Why it matters. It is the leading Indian Supreme Court case on privity. Jamna Das v. Ram Autar Pande (1911) Facts. A purchaser promised the seller to pay off the seller's mortgage debt. The mortgagee sued the purchaser on that promise. Principle. The mortgagee, not being a party to the sale, could not enforce the promise. (1911) 39 IA 7 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It applies privity to Indian law and is followed in M.C. Chacko .

law-of-contract-i-u1-t8.subtitle: Section 25 and section 185 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The general rule is "no consideration, no contract" . Section 25 says an agreement made without consideration is void . Section 25 itself makes three exceptions . A promise without consideration is still a contract if it is: in writing, registered, and made out of natural love and affection between near relations (Section 25(1)); a promise to compensate a person who voluntarily did something for the promisor in the past (Section 25(2)); or a written, signed promise to pay a time-barred debt (Section 25(3)). A gift actually made cannot be undone for want of consideration (Explanation 1). No consideration is needed to create an agency (Section 185). Examiners love this list. In real life, it explains when a family promise or a thank-you payment can be enforced.
legalProvision: Section 25. An agreement made without consideration is void, unless— (1) it is expressed in writing and registered under the law for the time being in force for the registration of documents, and is made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation to each other; or unless (2) it is a promise to compensate, wholly or in part, a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor, or something which the promisor was legally compellable to do; or unless (3) it is a promise, made in writing and signed by the person to be charged therewith, or by his agent generally or specially authorized in that behalf, to pay wholly or in part a debt of which the creditor might have enforced payment but for the law for the limitation of suits. In any of these cases, such an agreement is a contract. Explanation 1. Nothing in this section shall affect the validity, as between the donor and donee, of any gift actually made. Explanation 2. An agreement to which the consent of the promisor is freely given is not void merely because the consideration is inadequate; but the inadequacy of the consideration may be taken into account by the Court in determining the question whether the consent of the promisor was freely given.
Section 185. No consideration is necessary to create an agency.
Illustration (a) to Section 25. A promises, for no consideration, to give to B Rs. 1,000. This is a void agreement.
In simple words

The rule: a bare promise to give something for nothing is void. Exception 1: a family promise made out of love, if it is written and registered . Exception 2: a promise to pay someone who already helped you on his own . Exception 3: a written and signed promise to pay an old debt that can no longer be sued on. Explanation 1: a gift already handed over stays valid. Section 185: an agent can be appointed without consideration .
en.meaning:
An exception to consideration is a case where the law enforces a promise even though nothing was given in return for it. In each case Section 25 says: "such an agreement is a contract ". Why the law makes exceptions. The rule "no consideration, no contract" protects people from careless, one-sided promises. But in some cases there is good reason to enforce a promise without consideration. Love and affection within a family is a real reason. Writing and registration show the promise was serious. Gratitude for a past voluntary service rests on a real benefit already received. An old debt is still a moral duty. The law of limitation takes away only the remedy, not the debt itself. If it is in writing, registered, and made out of natural love and affection between near relations, it is a contract under Section 25(1). Otherwise, if it promises to compensate a past act done voluntarily for the promisor, or something he was legally compellable to do, Section 25(2). Otherwise, if it is a written, signed promise to pay a time-barred debt, Section 25(3). Otherwise, if a gift has already been made, the gift stands (Explanation 1). If it creates an agency, no consideration is needed (Section 185). Otherwise the agreement is void.
keyPoints: An agreement without consideration is void (Section 25). Section 25(1): written + registered + natural love and affection + near relation. Section 25(2): promise to compensate a past voluntary act done for the promisor, or what he was legally compellable to do. Section 25(3): written and signed promise to pay a time-barred debt , wholly or in part. A mere acknowledgment is not enough. Before the limitation period ends, a signed acknowledgment (Section 18) or an acknowledged payment (Section 19) of the Limitation Act gives a fresh period. Explanation 1: a completed gift stands. Explanation 2: inadequacy alone does not make an agreement void. Section 185: no consideration is needed for agency . Section 63: a promisee may remit performance without consideration. A subscription promise binds only after the promisee acts on it.

caseLaws.name: Rajlukhy Dabee v
caseLaws.facts: Bhootnath Mookerjee (1900) Facts. A husband agreed in writing to pay his wife a monthly allowance. The document recited their quarrels and her claim to live separately. Principle. The agreement was not made out of natural love and affection, and no consideration moved from the wife. (1900) 4 CWN 488. Why it matters. Section 25(1) needs real love and affection, not just a near relationship. Durga Prasad v. Baldeo (1880) Facts. Shops were built at the Collector's request. The occupying shopkeepers later promised a commission to the builder. Principle. No consideration, and not within Section 25(2), because the act was not done for the promisors. (1881) ILR 3 All 221. Why it matters. It marks the limit of Section 25(2): the act must be done for the promisor. Debi Prasad v. Bhagwati Prasad (1942) Facts. A debtor executed a document covering an old time-barred debt together with a small fresh advance, with interest. Principle. A mere acknowledgment of a debt, without more, is not enough under Section 25(3). There must be a promise to pay, express or implied. AIR 1943 All 63. Why it matters. It separates an acknowledgment from a promise to pay. Kedarnath Bhattacharji v. Gorie Mahomed (1886) Facts. The defendant signed for ₹100 towards a Town Hall at Howrah. Relying on the subscriptions, the Commissioners contracted with a builder. Principle. A subscriber who knows that liability will be incurred on the faith of his subscription is bound to pay. (1886) ILR 14 Cal 64. Why it matters. A charitable promise can be enforced once the promisee has acted on it. Abdul Aziz v. Masum Ali (1914) Facts. A person promised ₹500 for repairing a mosque. Nothing was done on the faith of the promise, and the committee sued his heirs. Principle. A mere gratuitous promise without consideration is not enforceable. (1914) ILR 36 All 268. Why it matters. It is the contrast case to Kedarnath .

selfTest.q: 1. What are the four conditions of Section 25(1)?
selfTest.a: Writing, registration, natural love and affection, and near relation.

selfTest.q: 2. A finds B's lost purse and returns it. B promises A Rs. 50. Is it enforceable?
selfTest.a: Yes. It is a promise to compensate a past voluntary act (Section 25(2), illustration (c)).

selfTest.q: 3. Is an oral promise to pay a time-barred debt valid?
selfTest.a: No. It must be in writing and signed (Section 25(3)).

selfTest.q: 4. Can a donor take back a completed gift because the donee gave nothing?
selfTest.a: No. A gift actually made is not affected by Section 25 (Explanation 1).

selfTest.q: 5. Which case held a charitable subscription enforceable, and why?
selfTest.a: Kedarnath Bhattacharji v. Gorie Mahomed , because the promisee took on liability on the faith of the subscription.

law-of-contract-i-u1-t11.subtitle: Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872; section 2(46) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019; section 10A of the Information Technology Act, 2000

en.inOneMinute: A standard form contract is a contract whose terms are printed or written in advance by one party (usually a big company, the State or a service provider) and offered to everyone on a "take it or leave it" basis. The other party cannot bargain; he can only sign, click or take the ticket. Railway and bus tickets, insurance policies, bank forms, courier consignment notes, dry-cleaning bills, builder-buyer agreements and website "I agree" terms are all standard forms. In the USA they are called "contracts of adhesion" ( LIC of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre ). Such contracts save time, but they are often used to slip in exemption clauses that cut down the stronger party's liability. The law protects the weaker party in five ways: Notice. A printed term binds only if reasonable notice of it was given before or at the time of the contract ( Parker ; Olley ; Thornton ). A mere receipt is not a contract document ( Chapelton ). Signature. A person who signs a document is normally bound by it, read or not ( L'Estrange v. Graucob ; Bharathi Knitting v. DHL ). Strict reading. An unclear term is read against the party who drafted it ( contra proferentem ). Unfair terms. Courts will not enforce an unfair and unreasonable clause imposed by a party with superior bargaining power; such a clause can be void under Section 23 as opposed to public policy ( Brojo Nath Ganguly ; Lilly White ). A clause barring the usual legal proceedings is void under Section 28 . Consumer law. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the State and National Commissions can declare an unfair contract term null and void (Sections 2(46), 49(2), 59(2)); Pioneer v. Govindan Raghavan applied this to a builder's one-sided agreement. Online terms accepted by clicking "I agree" are standard forms too; such contracts are valid under Section 10A of the IT Act, and the same protections apply. In the exam, define, give examples, then explain each protection with a case. In real life, this tells you when the "terms and conditions" on a bill, ticket or website really bind you.
legalProvision: There is no single section on standard form contracts . The rules come from case law and these provisions.

Section 23, Indian Contract Act, 1872. What considerations and objects are lawful, and what not. The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful, unless— it is forbidden by law; or is of such a nature that if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law; or is fraudulent ; or involves or implies injury to the person or property of another; or the Court regards it as immoral, or opposed to public policy. In each of these cases, the consideration or object of an agreement is said to be unlawful. Every agreement of which the object or consideration is unlawful is void.

Section 28, Indian Contract Act, 1872 (main part). Agreements in restraint of legal proceedings, void. Every agreement,— (a) by which any party thereto is restricted absolutely from enforcing his rights under or in respect of any contract, by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or which limits the time within which he may thus enforce his rights; or (b) which extinguishes the rights of any party thereto, or discharges any party thereto, from any liability, under or in respect of any contract on the expiry of a specified period so as to restrict any party from enforcing his rights, is void to the extent.

Section 10A, Information Technology Act, 2000. Validity of contracts formed through electronic means. Where in a contract formation, the communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, the revocation of proposals and acceptances, as the case may be, are expressed in electronic form or by means of an electronic records, such contract shall not be deemed to be unenforceable solely on the ground that such electronic form or means was used for that purpose.

Section 2(46), Consumer Protection Act, 2019. "unfair contract" means a contract between a manufacturer or trader or service provider on one hand, and a consumer on the other, having such terms which cause significant change in the rights of such consumer, including the following, namely:— (i) requiring manifestly excessive security deposits to be given by a consumer for the performance of contractual obligations; or (ii) imposing any penalty on the consumer, for the breach of contract thereof which is wholly disproportionate to the loss occurred due to such breach to the other party to the contract; or (iii) refusing to accept early repayment of debts on payment of applicable penalty; or (iv) entitling a party to the contract to terminate such contract unilaterally, without reasonable cause; or (v) permitting or has the effect of permitting one party to assign the contract to the detriment of the other party who is a consumer, without his consent; or (vi) imposing on the consumer any unreasonable charge, obligation or condition which puts such consumer to disadvantage;

Section 49(2), Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (1), the State Commission may also declare any terms of contract, which is unfair to any consumer, to be null and void.

Section 59(2), Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Without prejudice to sub-section (1), the National Commission may also declare any terms of contract, which is unfair to any consumer to be null and void.
In simple words

Section 23: an agreement (or a clause) whose object is opposed to public policy is void . The Supreme Court used this to strike down an unfair clause in a standard form ( Brojo Nath Ganguly ). Section 28: a clause that stops a party from going to court at all, or cuts down the time for suing, is void to that extent . Arbitration clauses are saved by the exceptions to the section. Section 10A, IT Act: a contract is not invalid merely because the offer and acceptance were made electronically , for example by clicking "I agree". Section 2(46), CPA 2019: an unfair contract is a contract between a trader or service provider and a consumer with terms that significantly change the consumer's rights , such as excessive deposits, disproportionate penalties or one-sided termination. Sections 49(2) and 59(2), CPA 2019: the State Commission and the National Commission can declare an unfair term null and void . A complaint that an unfair contract has been adopted is a "complaint" under Section 2(6)(i); such complaints go to the State Commission (consideration up to ₹10 crore, Section 47(1)(a)(ii)) or the National Commission (above ₹10 crore, Section 58(1)(a)(ii)).
en.meaning:
What a standard form contract is

A standard form contract is a contract in which:

the terms are drafted in advance by one party , usually in print or on a screen; the same terms are offered to every customer ; the other party has no real chance to bargain ; he must accept the whole form or go without the goods or service.

The Supreme Court described the position in LIC of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995): "In dotted line contracts there would be no occasion for a weaker party to bargain or to assume to have equal bargaining power. He has either to accept or leave the services or goods in terms of the dotted line contract."

Other names

Contract of adhesion: "In USA, the standard forms of contracts are called 'Contracts of Adhesion'" ( LIC ). The weaker party merely "adheres" to terms set by the other. Dotted line contract: the customer only signs "on the dotted line" ( Brojo Nath Ganguly ; Pioneer ). E-contracts: online standard forms. In a click-wrap contract the user clicks "I agree" after the terms are shown; in a browse-wrap contract the terms are only on a link and the site says that using it means accepting them; in a shrink-wrap contract the terms come inside the package of a product such as software.

Why they are used, and the danger

Advantages Dangers Saves time when thousands of similar contracts are made (railways, insurance, banks) The customer usually does not read the small print Same terms for everyone; easy to administer The drafter can insert exemption clauses limiting his liability Lower cost of each transaction Unequal bargaining power: "take it or leave it"

Running example

Priya gives a silk saree worth ₹12,000 to Sparkle Dry Cleaners for cleaning. She pays ₹300 and gets a printed bill. On the back, in small print: "Liability for loss or damage is limited to 10 times the cleaning charge." The saree is lost. Under the clause, Sparkle would pay only ₹3,000 (10 × ₹300), and Priya would lose ₹9,000 (₹12,000 − ₹3,000). Below we test whether the clause binds her.
keyPoints: Standard form: terms drafted by one party; "take it or leave it"; "contracts of adhesion" ( LIC ). Unsigned terms bind only with reasonable notice ( Parker ). Notice must be before or at the time of contract ( Olley ; Thornton ). A mere receipt is not a contract document ( Chapelton ). Signed terms bind, read or not ( L'Estrange ; Bharathi Knitting ). Contra proferentem : unclear terms read against the drafter. Unfair clause between unequal parties is void under Section 23 ( Brojo Nath Ganguly ). Clause barring courts is void under Section 28 ; arbitration saved. CPA 2019: State and National Commissions may declare unfair terms null and void (Sections 49(2), 59(2)); Pioneer . Click-wrap contracts are valid (IT Act, Section 10A).

caseLaws.name: Parker v
caseLaws.facts: South Eastern Railway Co. (1877) Facts. Parker left a bag in a railway cloakroom, paid 2d and received a ticket whose back limited the company's liability to £10. The bag was lost. Principle. An unsigned ticket's conditions bind if the company gave reasonable notice of them, even if the customer did not read them. (1877) 2 CPD 416 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It is the leading case on the reasonable notice test. L'Estrange v. F. Graucob Ltd. (1934) Facts. A café owner signed an order form for a slot machine; small print excluded all warranties. The machine did not work. Principle. A person who signs a contractual document is bound by it, whether or not he has read it. [1934] 2 KB 394. Why it matters. It is the leading case on signed standard forms . Lilly White v. R. Munuswami (1964) Facts. A customer's new saree (Rs. 220) was lost by a dry cleaner whose bill limited liability to 50% of the market price. Principle. Such a term "cannot be enforced by a court, merely, because it is printed on the reverse of a bill." AIR 1966 Mad 13 (Madras High Court). Why it matters. It is the Indian authority against unreasonable printed exemption clauses . Bharathi Knitting Co. v. DHL Worldwide Express Courier (1996) Facts. The sender signed a courier consignment note limiting the courier's liability to US$100. Principle. "When there is a specific term in the contract, the parties are bound by the terms in the contract." (1996) 4 SCC 704. Why it matters. It applies the signature rule in India. Central Inland Water Transport Corporation v. Brojo Nath Ganguly (1986) Facts. A Government company's service rule let it terminate permanent employees on three months' notice or pay, without reasons. Ganguly's services were terminated under it on 26 February 1983. Principle. The Courts will "strike down an unfair and unreasonable contract, or an unfair and unreasonable clause in a contract, entered into between parties who are not equal in bargaining power"; such a clause is void under Section 23. AIR 1986 SC 1571 : (1986) 3 SCC 156. Why it matters. It is the leading Indian case on unconscionable terms in standard forms . LIC of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995) Facts. LIC's term insurance policy under Table 58 was offered only to persons in Government, quasi-Government or reputed commercial firms. The condition was challenged as discriminatory. Principle. "In dotted line contracts there would be no occasion for a weaker party to bargain"; the restricting clause was unconstitutional and severable, and LIC's terms must be reasonable, just and fair. AIR 1995 SC 1811 : (1995) 5 SCC 482. Why it matters. It explains standard form ("adhesion") contracts and the weaker party's lack of choice. Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. v. Govindan Raghavan (2019) Facts. A builder's agreement charged the buyer 18% interest a year for delayed payments but gave the buyer only 9% a year for the builder's delay in possession. Principle. "A term of a contract will not be final and binding if it is shown that the flat purchasers had no option but to sign on the dotted line, on a contract framed by the builder." [2019] 5 SCR 1169. Why it matters. It applies the protection against one-sided standard forms to consumer contracts .

law-of-contract-i-u1-t3.subtitle: Sections 2(b), 7, 8 and 9 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Acceptance is the "yes" that turns an offer into a promise. Under Section 2(b), when the person to whom a proposal is made signifies his assent to it, the proposal is accepted, and a proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise . To be valid, the acceptance must be absolute and unqualified , expressed in a usual and reasonable manner or in the manner the offer prescribes (Section 7), communicated to the offeror, and given by the offeree while the offer is still open . Acceptance may be by words or by conduct , including by performing the conditions of the offer (Sections 8, 9). Silence is not acceptance. In exams, marks come from the definition, Section 7 quoted, each essential with a case ( Hyde v. Wrench , Felthouse v. Bindley , Carlill , Powell v. Lee , Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar ), and the counter-offer rule. In real life, it tells you whether your reply closed the deal or only opened a new round of bargaining.
legalProvision: Section 2(b). When the person to whom the proposal is made signifies his assent thereto, the proposal is said to be accepted. A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise;

Section 7. Acceptance must be absolute. In order to convert a proposal into a promise, the acceptance must— (1) be absolute and unqualified; (2) be expressed in some usual and reasonable manner, unless the proposal prescribes the manner in which it is to be accepted. If the proposal prescribes a manner in which it is to be accepted, and the acceptance is not made in such manner, the proposer may, within a reasonable time after the acceptance is communicated to him, insist that his proposal shall be accepted in the prescribed manner, and not otherwise; but if he fails to do so, he accepts the acceptance.

Section 8. Acceptance by performing conditions, or receiving consideration. Performance of the conditions of a proposal, or the acceptance of any consideration for a reciprocal promise which may be offered with a proposal, is an acceptance of the proposal.

Section 9. Promises, express and implied. In so far as the proposal or acceptance of any promise is made in words, the promise is said to be express. In so far as such proposal or acceptance is made otherwise than in words, the promise is said to be implied.

Section 3 (relevant part). The communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, and the revocation of proposals and acceptances, respectively, are deemed to be made by any act or omission of the party proposing, accepting or revoking by which he intends to communicate such proposal, acceptance or revocation, or which has the effect of communicating it.

Section 6 (relevant part). A proposal is revoked— … (2) by the lapse of the time prescribed in such proposal for its acceptance, or, if no time is so prescribed, by the lapse of a reasonable time, without communication of the acceptance; (3) by the failure of the acceptor to fulfil a condition precedent to acceptance; …
In simple words

Section 2(b): acceptance is the offeree showing his assent . Once he does, the offer becomes a promise . Section 7(1): the "yes" must be complete . A "yes, but …" is not acceptance. Section 7(2): accept in a normal, reasonable way , or in the way the offer asks . If the offeree uses another way, the offeror must object within a reasonable time ; if he keeps quiet, the acceptance stands. Section 8: doing what the offer asks (or taking the consideration offered) is acceptance. Section 9: acceptance can be express (in words) or implied (by conduct). Section 3: acceptance is made by an act or omission meant to communicate it. Section 6(2), (3): acceptance must come before the offer lapses , and after any condition precedent is fulfilled.
en.meaning:
What acceptance does

Acceptance is the second half of an agreement. Offer + acceptance = promise (Section 2(b)) = agreement (Section 2(e)). At the moment of acceptance the offeror loses the freedom to walk away, so the law insists that the acceptance be clear and complete.

Section 2(b) broken into parts

Words of Section 2(b) What it means "the person to whom the proposal is made" Only the offeree can accept (for a general offer , any member of the public who knows of it) "signifies" The assent must be shown outwardly, by words or conduct; a decision kept in one's mind is not enough "his assent thereto " Agreement to that proposal , on its terms "A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise" The moment of acceptance is the moment of agreement

Why the law insists on these rules

If a changed reply counted as acceptance, the offeror would be bound to terms he never offered. If a secret decision counted, the offeror would never know whether he was bound. If silence counted, anyone could force a contract on another by a letter.

Running example

Meena writes to Ravi : "I will sell you my sewing machine, model XL-200, for ₹8,000 . Delivery at my house on Sunday. Reply by letter by Friday. " The letter reaches Ravi on Tuesday.

We will look at several replies Ravi might give and test each against the rules.
keyPoints: Acceptance = signifying assent to a proposal; the proposal then becomes a promise (Section 2(b)). It must be absolute and unqualified (Section 7(1)); a changed reply is a counter-offer that kills the original offer ( Hyde v. Wrench ). It must follow the prescribed manner , or a usual and reasonable one; an offeror who does not object in reasonable time accepts the acceptance (Section 7(2)). It must be communicated ; a mental decision is not enough ( Felthouse v. Bindley ), and it must come from the offeree or his authorised agent ( Powell v. Lee ). It can be by conduct or performance (Sections 8, 9; Carlill ; Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar ). It must be given while the offer is open (Section 6). Silence is not acceptance. In auctions subject to confirmation, the contract is complete only on confirmation ( Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram ).

caseLaws.name: Hyde v
caseLaws.facts: Wrench (1840) Facts. Wrench offered to sell his farm for £1,000. Hyde's agent offered £950, which Wrench later refused. Hyde then tried to accept the £1,000 offer. Principle. A counter-offer rejects the original offer, which cannot afterwards be revived by an acceptance. (1840) 49 ER 132. Why it matters. It is the leading case on absolute acceptance and counter-offers (Section 7(1)). Felthouse v. Bindley (1862) Facts. An uncle offered to buy his nephew's horse for £30 15s, saying he would treat it as his if he heard no more. The nephew decided to sell but never told him; the horse was sold at auction by mistake. Principle. Acceptance must be communicated to the offeror; silence is not acceptance. 142 ER 1037 : (1862) 11 CB (NS) 869. Why it matters. It shows that a mental decision to accept is not enough. Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893) Facts. The company advertised a £100 reward to anyone who caught influenza after using its smoke ball as directed. Mrs Carlill used it and caught influenza. Principle. A general offer can be accepted by performing its conditions; the offeror may dispense with notice of acceptance. [1893] 1 QB 256 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It illustrates acceptance by performance (Section 8). Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar v. Union of India (2006) Facts. The Railways sent cheques for Rs. 9,111 and Rs. 9,032 against larger claims, stating that encashment would be full and final settlement. The claimant encashed them without prior protest and then sued for the balance. Principle. Encashing the cheques was acceptance by conduct of the offer of full and final settlement; the offeree cannot change his mind afterwards. (2006) 5 SCC 311 : AIR 2006 SC 2331. Why it matters. It is the leading Indian Supreme Court case on acceptance by conduct . Powell v. Lee (1908) Facts. School managers resolved to appoint Powell as headmaster. One manager, without authority, told him of the decision; the managers later appointed someone else. Principle. Acceptance must be communicated by the offeree or his authorised agent; unauthorised information is not acceptance. (1908) 99 LT 284. Why it matters. It shows who must communicate the acceptance. Union of India v. Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram (1969) Facts. The highest bid of Rs. 4,01,000 at an auction of a liquor licence needed the Chief Commissioner's confirmation, which was never given. Principle. Where a bid is subject to confirmation, the contract is complete only on confirmation, not on the fall of the hammer. AIR 1971 SC 2295 : (1970) 2 SCR 594. Why it matters. It shows when acceptance happens in auctions subject to approval.

selfTest.q: 1. What is acceptance under the Act?
selfTest.a: When the person to whom a proposal is made signifies his assent to it (Section 2(b)).

selfTest.q: 2. Meena offers delivery at her house. Ravi replies, "I accept at ₹8,000, delivery at my house." Is this acceptance?
selfTest.a: No. Changing the place of delivery is a new term, so the reply is a counter-offer (Section 7(1)); it rejects Meena's offer ( Hyde v. Wrench ).

selfTest.q: 3. The offer says "reply by letter". The offeree replies by email, and the offeror does nothing. Is there a contract?
selfTest.a: Yes. Under Section 7(2), the offeror who fails to insist on the prescribed manner within a reasonable time accepts the acceptance.

selfTest.q: 4. After making a counter-offer, can the offeree accept the original offer?
selfTest.a: No. The counter-offer rejected it ( Hyde v. Wrench ).

selfTest.q: 5. Is encashing a cheque sent "in full and final settlement" an acceptance?
selfTest.a: Yes, acceptance by conduct, if done without protest ( Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar v. Union of India ).

selfTest.q: 6. Is the highest bid at an auction subject to confirmation a concluded contract?
selfTest.a: No, not until it is confirmed ( Union of India v. Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram ).
